images.title: Any crossing angle still gives right angles
images.purpose: Shows that equal diagonals bisecting each other at 40° still make every corner 70° + 20° = 90°.
images.composition: Plain white background, the main object large and centred with wide empty margins, no scenery, no characters, no extra decoration. One wide rectangle in the centre with its diagonals crossing, the angles at O and at one corner marked, and one short sum under the shape.
images.exact_structure: One rectangle ABCD in dark outline, about 2.75 times as wide as it is tall, with A top left, B top right, C bottom right and D bottom left. The diagonals AC and BD are thick teal (#0072B2) lines crossing at O; each of the four half diagonals carries one identical short dark tick mark. At O, inside the left triangle AOD, a small amber (#E69F00) arc labelled 40°; at O, inside the top triangle AOB, a larger amber arc labelled 140°. At corner A two small reddish purple (#CC79A7) arcs: one between side AD and diagonal AC labelled 70°, and one between side AB and diagonal AC labelled 20°. Under the rectangle, centred, the line 70° + 20° = 90°. Only corner A is lettered: the letter A sits just outside the top left corner; the other corners carry no letters. Nothing else in the frame.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
images.takeaway: Whatever the angle between equal bisecting diagonals, each corner adds up to 90°.
images.description: Shows that equal diagonals bisecting each other at 40° still make every corner 70° + 20° = 90°.
images.context: Isosceles ∆AOD: base angles (180 − 40) ÷ 2 = 70; isosceles ∆AOB: base angles (180 − 140) ÷ 2 = 20; corner A = 70 + 20 = 90.

image_decisions.why: Marking 40° at the crossing and 70° plus 20° at a corner makes the any angle argument visible.
